title: You’re not actually afraid of the battle.
paragraphs: You’re not actually afraid of the battle.
You’re afraid of what you don’t see.
Because what you can’t see feels more dangerous than what you can.
And that’s exactly where the enemy traps you.
You saw the closed doors, the sickness, the lack, the opposition.
But what if your fear isn’t coming from your situation…
What if it’s coming from your blindness?
Because in that moment—when the servant woke up and saw an army surrounding them—he wasn’t wrong.
There was a real reason to panic.
But he still wasn’t seeing the full story.
This is where most people live.
You know God is real… but you don’t see Him in your situation.
You believe He is powerful… but your circumstances feel louder.
You’ve heard His promises… but your emotions preach a different gospel.
And suddenly, the visible feels more true than the eternal.
“Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.” — 2 Kings 6:16
That statement makes no sense… unless you see what he sees.
And then comes the prayer that changes everything:

“Then Elisha prayed and said, ‘O Lord, please open his eyes that he may see.’ So the Lord opened the eyes of the young man, and he saw, and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.” — 2 Kings 6:17
God didn’t remove the threat first.
Your greatest problem might not be what’s around you…
But what you’re unable—or unwilling—to see.
It makes temporary things feel ultimate.
It makes you forget that God is already present, already working, already surrounding you.
And sometimes, the reason you feel overwhelmed isn’t because God has left…
It’s because you’ve stopped seeing Him.
Some scholars interpret this passage not just as a miracle of sight—but as a revelation of reality that was already there.
Because how often do we live like spiritual orphans…
When heaven is already surrounding us?
How often do we trust our feelings more than His Word?
“The god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers…” — 2 Corinthians 4:4
And if the enemy can’t destroy you…
He’ll make you focus on the army instead of the God who commands heaven’s armies.
He’ll make you obsess over your failure instead of the cross that paid for it.
He’ll make you feel alone when you’re actually surrounded.
Jesus didn’t just come to forgive sin.
“The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me… to proclaim recovery of sight to the blind…” — Luke 4:18
But the cross says something completely different.
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
He didn’t wait for you to see clearly.
So you could finally see the light.
“I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” — John 8:12
So now the question is not:
Will you ask Him to open your eyes?
Because before God shows you the armies of heaven…
He often shows you the condition of your heart.
Not shame that pushes you away…
But conviction that pulls you closer.
“Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out.” — Acts 3:19
You don’t need a new circumstance first.
You don’t need to escape everything around you.
You need to encounter the God who is already there.
So pray this—not casually, but desperately:
Open my eyes to Your presence.
Open my eyes to my sin.
Open my eyes to Your grace.
Open my eyes to the cross.
Because once you see Him rightly…
If this stirred something in you, don’t ignore it.
From fear to faith. From blindness to sight. From shame to redemption.
